title: WHAT IF YOU JUMPED ON EVERY WORLD?

segments.line: Pitch black space.
Dusty rock under your sneakers.
You crouch for a normal hop,
push off, and keep rising.
Higher and higher.
The comet shrinks below your feet.
Jump here and you never come back down.
From worlds that launch you over houses
to worlds that flatten you instantly:
what if you jumped on every world?
(Title Card: WHAT IF YOU JUMPED ON EVERY WORLD?)
Start with your Earth baseline.
Stand in your school gym, crouch,
and pop up beside the chalk wall.
Slap! About half a metre.
Outside in a floodlit stadium
sits the high jump world record:
two point four five metres,
set by Javier Sotomayor in nineteen ninety three.
Even the best human barely clears a
doorway. Unless we leave Earth.
(Chapter 2 Card)
Step onto your bathroom scale,
because a single rule runs this whole tour.
Your leg muscles pack the same push everywhere.
Only gravity changes.
Less gravity means a higher
jump and a longer hang time.
More gravity drags you straight down.
Ready to test that rule?
Look out your window tonight.
(Chapter 3 Card)
Touch down on the Moon under a starry
sky with blue Earth overhead.
Lunar gravity pulls at about one point
six two metres per second squared.
Push off with your gym hop and boing!
You soar about three metres high,
floating for nearly four seconds
before drifting softly into the grey dust.
Wait: why did real astronauts barely hop?
(Chapter 4 Card)
Time for an Apollo reality check.
Real astronauts wore stiff bulky spacesuits
and heavy life support backpacks.
Bending their knees felt like wrestling a giant mattress,
so they jumped far less than our no suit leap.
In nineteen seventy two,
Charlie Duke tried a big high jump,
tipped backwards in slow motion,
and fell flat onto his backpack!
Next stop: grab a basketball.
(Chapter 5 Card)
Welcome to the rusty red court of Mars,
where gravity sits at about three point
seven one metres per second squared.
Dribble through red dust,
plant your sneakers, and launch.
You rise about two point six times higher than on Earth,
gliding above the rim for an easy slam dunk!
Want that exact same bounce somewhere
way stranger? Head toward the Sun.
(Chapter 6 Card)
Cratered Mercury looks tiny,
yet its dense core gives it basically
the same gravity pull as Mars.
You leap just as high over silver rock.
Then you unfold a chair to watch
the sunrise before jumping again.
You wait. And you wait.
A solar day on Mercury lasts about four thousand,
two hundred and twenty two hours.
Pack snacks, because the next planet cooks them.
(Chapter 7 Card)
Drop beneath the yellow clouds of Venus
and forget jumping altogether.
Thick air crushes down
at about ninety three times Earth's surface pressure,
like being about nine hundred metres
underwater without a submarine.
Worse, the rocks bake
at about four hundred and sixty five degrees Celsius.
You do not jump here:
you get squished like a panini and cooked!
Could a robot survive?
(Chapter 8 Card)
Engineers tried. Tough
Soviet Venera probes parachuted
down inside heavy titanium shells
just to photograph that glowing landscape.
The moment a lander touched the ground,
a brutal countdown clock started.
Tick, tick, sizzle.
Even the longest lasting Soviet probe
survived only about two hours on the surface
before Venus fried it silent.
Let us cool off somewhere thick air actually helps.
(Chapter 9 Card)
Out around Saturn orbits hazy golden Titan.
Gravity here pulls at only about one seventh of Earth's,
while the cold surface air
is about four times denser than ours.
Tape cardboard wings to your arms,
hop off an icy boulder, and flap hard!
Those homemade wings catch the soupy air
and lift you airborne above dark lakes.
Feeling unstoppable? Try Jupiter.
(Chapter 10 Card)
Bad news: giant striped Jupiter
has no solid surface at all,
so we hang a diving board in its upper clouds.
At about two point five times Earth's
gravity, your knees groan.
A seventy kilogram you weighs
like about one hundred and sixty five kilograms on Earth.
You strain, hop about twenty centimetres,
land, and sink straight into the clouds!
At least the next giant floats.
(Chapter 11 Card)
Ringed Saturn has no solid floor either,
though near its clouds your weight feels close to home.
Instead, Saturn hides
a wild party trick.
On average, it has a density of about six hundred and
eighty seven kilograms per cubic metre,
less dense than water!
Fill a giant bathtub,
drop Saturn in beside a rubber duck,
and the planet floats.
Now grab a bowling ball.
(Chapter 12 Card)
Step into the outer solar system's
ice giant bowling alley.
Down the left lane rolls pale cyan Uranus,
spinning tipped right over on its side
at about ninety eight degrees like a tumbling barrel.
Hop near its clouds and you
bounce slightly easier than home.
Try deep blue Neptune next
door, though, and oof:
Neptune pulls a bit harder than Earth.
Ready for superhero mode?
(Chapter 13 Card)
Land on icy Pluto,
where the Sun shrinks to a bright star
over a heart shaped glacier.
Gravity drops to about zero
point six two metres per second squared,
so a seventy kilogram you weighs
like about four to five kilograms on Earth.
Push off and you rocket about seven metres high,
clearing a house with roughly nine seconds of airtime!
Tiny worlds get wilder still.
(Chapter 14 Card)
Tiptoe onto Dimorphos,
a rubble asteroid only about one hundred and
fifty one metres wide.
It is so small NASA
used it for target practice:
in twenty twenty two,
the DART spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos
and shortened its orbit by about thirty three minutes.
Gravity here barely whispers.
Even a tiny flinch sends you floating up,
leading straight back to where we started.
(Chapter 15 Card)
Remember our opening comet?
When the European Space Agency set
its Philae lander onto comet sixty seven P,
its harpoons failed.
Philae bounced off at about thirty eight
centimetres per second, slower than a stroll,
yet flew for about one kilometre
over nearly two hours!
Your jump is much faster than that bounce.
Push off here, wave goodbye,
and off you go into space forever.
(Chapter 16 Card)
Final boss: the Sun.
Give yourself magic heat proof boots
and an imaginary platform at the solar surface.
Solar gravity slams down
at about twenty eight times Earth's pull.
Forget jumping: you could not even stand!
Your knees buckle, your face pancakes onto the deck,
and wiggling a thumb feels heroic.
Suddenly, ordinary Earth sounds pretty wonderful.
(Chapter 17 Card)
Back on your city rooftop at dawn, take a little hop.
About half a metre up,
soft thud down.
Your tiny Earth jump suddenly feels perfect.
And you can spot part of this tour yourself:
Mars and Jupiter appear
very close together in the mid November sky,
and the Leonid meteors peak around the seventeenth
and eighteenth of November, so look up.
Which world would you jump on first?
(End Card: IFMOSPHERE · Comment your world · Subscribe)
